sentences.text: IPTC Metawatch is the International Press Telecommunications Council's free, open monitor of whether news publishers keep the credits, captions and rights information embedded in their photographs, checked every month across more than 500 publishers in 122 countries (IPTC announcement, 5 October 2026); the provenance census record types it as a monitor of the media lineage whose capability is to test, its provenance object 'the lead photograph of a news article, as served to the reader', its operator the IPTC at metawatch.iptc.org (provenance census record).

Its own overview states the object from the side of the carrier: Metawatch 'tracks how often major news publishers preserve embedded photo metadata' — Exif, IPTC Photo Metadata in its IIM and XMP forms, and C2PA — and scores the photographs a curated list of publishers serves (Metawatch overview), the carrier the census record names as 'embedded metadata (Exif, IPTC IIM and XMP) and C2PA manifests' (provenance census record).

Content Credentials stand in the first of the dimensions of provenance the archive's provenance packet distinguishes: frameworks for the artifact (C2PA / Content Credentials) and for the corpus 'are not designed to address the survival of authorial lineage through AI synthesis', artifact provenance verifying that 'this file' was created by 'this source' at 'this time', at the moment of creation (#725); the same packet places IPTC AI metadata at 'Layer 1 metadata', 'Disclosure, not lineage' (#725).

On the first of each month its crawler visits 508 news publishers in 122 countries, takes up to 20 recent articles from each and reads the lead photograph of every article, checking Exif, IPTC Photo Metadata and C2PA Content Credentials and scoring creator, caption, copyright and credit line, 'the “4 Cs”' (IPTC announcement); the census record's unit is 'a news publisher, sampled each month through up to 20 recent articles', its count 508 publishers in 122 countries as of October 2026, monthly on the first, its relation types creator, credit, copyright, caption, the PLUS data-mining preference and Content Credentials (provenance census record); the per-field page calls the four scored fields 'the "Four Cs" of news photo provenance', the others tracked for context (Metawatch per-field breakdown).

The crawler is 'deliberately light', about 40 to 60 requests per publisher a month, honouring robots.txt and keeping no article text or image files, and every run is published as open data under CC BY 4.0, new results appearing on the first of every month (IPTC announcement); the overview names it 'A project of the International Press Telecommunications Council', its data CC BY 4.0, with an opt-out for publishers by email (Metawatch overview), and the census record carries 'every run published as open data' under 'CC BY 4.0 (each run's data)' (provenance census record).

What it tests is a transformation: credits 'are lost between camera and reader' as content management systems re-encode images, delivery networks resize them and optimisation tools discard what looks like unnecessary bytes, and once an image is copied or collected by an AI crawler its embedded metadata 'is often the only record of where it came from and on what terms it may be used' (IPTC announcement); the census record names the transformation tested 'publication through a news site's pipeline (CMS, CDN, image optimisation)' (provenance census record).

The archive's packet states the loss one layer on: 'A C2PA-signed image whose caption is rewritten by a model that strips the photographer's name has lost semantic provenance even though artifact provenance is preserved', the dimensions being independent, so that 'Solving any one dimension does not solve the others' (#725).

Metawatch builds on IMATAG's 2018 State of Image Metadata study and the IPTC's own prototype crawler of 2019, and differs in measuring every month (IPTC announcement; the census record quotes the sentence as its lineage evidence, provenance census record), and the census record relates it as part of the IPTC's photo-metadata tests, beside the census's C2PA conformance entry, while keeping it apart from the earlier test: 'NOT the 2019 IPTC social-media test: it measures news publishers monthly' (provenance census record).

Its overview dates five runs, the first on 2026-06-03 and then monthly to 2026-10-01 (Metawatch overview), and the announcement counts 294 publishers 'measured every month since June' (IPTC announcement).

The IPTC's post of 8 September 2026 reports that at the 2026 Photo Metadata Conference, held 'Last Thursday', Brendan Quinn 'appeared again to introduce Metawatch', 'IPTC’s new public service that monitors real-world usage of metadata in images across the global news industry, tracking IPTC/XMP, C2PA, AI opt-outs and more' (IPTC, 8 September 2026); Paul Melcher's LinkedIn post of 14 September 2026, read by its card alone, says the IPTC 'now publishes Metawatch' (LinkedIn card); the conference took as its focus AI transparency and content provenance, 'tracking real-world adoption of content transparency technologies by AI engines, news sites, software and services' (IPTC, 8 September 2026).

The announcement is dated 5 October 2026 and is the newest post under the IPTC's Photo Metadata tag (IPTC announcement; Photo Metadata archive); the census record's lifecycle is active, 'announced 5 October 2026', its founding given the same way, the run reported for October 2026 and the record read on 2026-10-29 (provenance census record).

The Capture Registry records the difference: the record 'dates the monitor by its announcement, 5 October 2026', two cards date it earlier, the IPTC post of 8 September and Melcher's post of 14 September, and the September showing is carried at the capture 'unchecked against the posts themselves' (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29).

In the October run 7.2% of editorial images carried a credit or copyright notice, against IMATAG's 8% in 2018, so that keeping the photographer's credit attached 'has not improved'; 321 of the 425 publishers it could crawl kept none of the scored IPTC fields; 11% of 6,580 images carried any IPTC metadata, the photographer's name on 7.9%, the credit line on 5.7%, copyright on 5.6% (IPTC announcement); the census record's retention results carry the 7.2% and the 321 of 425 with the 27 of 6,580 images bearing a C2PA manifest (provenance census record), and the announcement reads its first results as showing 'how little has changed since 2018' and why metadata 'matters more than ever now that AI companies are crawling the web' (IPTC announcement).

The overview gives the latest run as 2026-10-01, 425 sites, 122 countries and 6,580 images, a mean IPTC score of 5.96, 11% with any IPTC and 0.5% with C2PA, and says that 'Any average describes almost nobody here' (Metawatch overview); the per-field page counts over 6,514 images, Creator at 7.9%, CreditLine 5.7%, Copyright 5.3%, CaptionDescription 5%, the licensing fields below 3% (Metawatch per-field breakdown), so that copyright stands at 5.6% in the announcement and at 5.3% on the per-field page.

On where the loss happens the operator's pages differ in emphasis: the announcement finds 'It isn’t the CDN’s fault', images through Cloudflare, Akamai, CloudFront and Fastly losing their metadata 87% to 95% of the time and images with no CDN 87%, so that 'Stripping appears to happen in the publishing pipeline', the fix 'usually a setting, not a project' (IPTC announcement; the census record quotes the pipeline sentence as its evidence, provenance census record), while the per-field page reads its dataset as 'publishers and CDNs are discarding metadata that the photographers and agencies almost certainly embedded upstream' (Metawatch per-field breakdown).

The archive's specification for machine-eligible handwritten artifacts embeds IPTC Creator (the author or heteronym), Credit, CopyrightNotice, Headline, Description and DateCreated in every published derivative, with an XMP mirror and C2PA manifests wrapping the IPTC/EXIF assertions (#1409); it records embedded IPTC photo metadata as extracted by Google and travelling with the image, its composition role unknown, 'scaffold the pipeline provably reads' (#1409); and it carries the same fields in a visible membrane because 'physically embodied metadata survives screenshot, rehosting, filename change, metadata stripping, PDF embedding, and sidecar loss', under a triple redundancy of pixels, embedded IPTC/XMP/C2PA and external records (#1409).

The archive's identifier stamp for a lossless image sits in its EXIF ImageDescription or UserComment (#1432), and its self-audit protocol plans a 'Hash/signature manifest (C2PA-compatible) binding provenance claims to deposited objects' (#204).

Some publishers moved: USA Today from no credit metadata in 2019 to 95% of its lead photographs carrying credit, creator and copyright in September, Les Echos from 6% to 75%, and across the 294 publishers measured monthly since June those keeping any metadata rose from 60 to 67; France led October at 19.8 of 100, ahead of Germany at 19.2, with only countries of more than three scored publishers ranked (IPTC announcement).

Of 505 publishers whose policies were checked, 234 block at least one AI crawler in robots.txt, but 'robots.txt protects a website, not a photograph', and the PLUS Data Mining field appears on 0.6% of images (IPTC announcement); the archive's training-layer protocol holds that robots.txt and C2PA, which it does not call useless, operate 'primarily at the publication / legal / evidentiary layer rather than at the training-survival layer' (#127).

Leaving out the IPTC's own site, 27 of 6,580 images carried a C2PA manifest, all but one signed by an AI or design tool and none 'from a camera or a newsroom’s own signing', and seven carried a Digital Source Type disclosing generative-AI editing, so that, in the announcement's reading, provenance in news photography 'is arriving first through the tools that make synthetic images' (IPTC announcement); the per-field page finds DigitalSourceType on 0.2% of images and the AI prompt and AI system fields on none (Metawatch per-field breakdown), properties the IPTC Photo Metadata Standard added for AI-generated content on 27 November 2025 (Photo Metadata archive).

The archive's packet calls the adoption of artifact authenticity 'uneven' and C2PA's ingredient assertions 'optional, under-adopted' (#725), and its field manual holds that C2PA standards and watermarking have not 'achieved sufficient adoption to function as infrastructure' (#499).

The archive reads C2PA's trust as a device's: C2PA 'attests what a device reports having done' where a content-derived identifier 'computes what the bytes are', validation optional in the first, the two complementary (#1443), C2PA anchoring in device and issuer certificates and the AXN regime in content derivation and a public ledger (#1409), C2PA securing 'the camera's testimony, not the author's' (#1444).

It declares a nonsynthetic capture by the IPTC DigitalSourceType inside the file, 'in the same controlled vocabulary whose trainedAlgorithmicMedia value marks the synthetic class', and holds that 'C2PA, FADGI, and IPTC provenance vocabularies are the same insight arriving as standards' (#1409).

The monitor states its limits: the United States slipped from first to fourth in October because AP and USA Today 'began blocking automated access this month', 'a reminder that bot-blocking aimed at AI also shuts out research' (IPTC announcement; quoted in the census record's evidence, provenance census record), and publishers reached without a photograph are listed as no_images rather than scored zero, 'usually our blind spot rather than their practice' (Metawatch overview); the census record leaves unchecked 'the Metawatch site itself and its published run data' and IMATAG's 2018 study, and marks the monitor 'NOT a C2PA verifier' (provenance census record).

The archive holds the artifact dimension necessary and insufficient: C2PA 'prevents forgery; it does not constitute authorship' (#729), 'C2PA authenticates media' and does not cover text (#621), and 'When a 5,000-word article becomes a 200-word AI Overview, C2PA cannot tell you what was lost' (#615).

It finds that metadata standards, C2PA among them, do not address the measurable reception consequences of provenance and attribution (#833), that provenance and attribution studies, C2PA among them, 'have focused on attribution loss in AI outputs' (#1003), and that cross-format content provenance standards give 'starting points for the public and machine-readable layers' (#95).

On Google's AI Overview, signed out, on 2026-10-29, the Capture Registry finds the method and scale right ('Every month', 'more than 500 news publishers in 122 countries' and the fields are the announcement's own) and 'Free and open' matched to the census record's licence quote, checked against that record and the pages it saved (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29).

It finds the findings absent, 'The composition gives what the monitor checks and none of what it found', and the access limit not composed; it reads the Overview first as naming 'the maker, the method and the scale of a monitor three weeks old', then as composing 'A new provenance monitor' 'at the grain of its feature list', when what it measures is 'the erasure of credit in the publishing pipeline', carrying 'the instrument' and leaving out 'its reading', the IPTC photo metadata capture's pattern 'in small: the carrier composed, the loss omitted' (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29).

At the capture the IPTC is named, Paul Melcher and Brendan Quinn appear only in cards, no identifier is given and the monitor's own pages are cited, and no card cites the census record, which landed on provenanceerasure.org the same day (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29).

The census record asks of each entity 'What provenance does this system carry, through which operation, on whose assertion, with what evidence of survival?', each quote verbatim from a saved source, and for Metawatch read one source, the announcement, on 2026-10-29 (provenance census record); Wikipedia has no article on IPTC Metawatch and no article text naming it beside the IPTC, and its article on the operator, which does not name Metawatch, describes the IPTC as 'a consortium of the world's major news agencies, other news providers and news industry vendors' acting as 'the global standards body of the news media', whose photo metadata, the IIM set that XMP has largely superseded, is 'by far IPTC's most widely used standard' (Wikipedia).

sentences.text: The IPTC describes Metawatch as a free, open monitor that checks every month whether more than 500 news publishers in 122 countries keep the credits, captions and rights information embedded in their photographs (IPTC announcement, 5 October 2026).

Its overview says Metawatch tracks how often major news publishers preserve embedded photo metadata (Exif, IPTC Photo Metadata in IIM and XMP, and C2PA), crawling a curated list monthly; it is a project of the IPTC, its data licensed CC BY 4.0 (Metawatch overview).

Each month the crawler visits 508 publishers in 122 countries, takes up to 20 recent articles from each and reads the lead photograph, checking Exif, IPTC and C2PA and scoring the 4 Cs, creator, caption, copyright and credit line, the per-field page's 'Four Cs' of news photo provenance; the crawler is light, every run is open data, and results appear on the first of the month (IPTC announcement; per-field breakdown).

The announcement explains the problem as credits lost between camera and reader through re-encoding, resizing and optimisation, and says embedded metadata is often the only record of an image's origin and terms once it is copied or crawled for AI; its first results show little change since 2018 (IPTC announcement).
It builds on IMATAG's 2018 study and the IPTC's 2019 prototype crawler and differs in measuring monthly (IPTC announcement).

Its runs run from 2026-06-03 to 2026-10-01 (overview); it was introduced by Brendan Quinn at the 2026 Photo Metadata Conference, reported on 8 September 2026 (IPTC), Paul Melcher's LinkedIn card of 14 September says the IPTC now publishes it, and the announcement is dated 5 October 2026, the newest post under the Photo Metadata tag.

In October 7.2% of editorial images carried a credit or copyright notice (IMATAG 2018: 8%), 321 of 425 crawlable publishers kept no scored field and 11% of 6,580 images carried any IPTC metadata (IPTC announcement; overview), with copyright at 5.6% in the announcement and 5.3% of 6,514 images on the per-field page, and even Creator below one image in ten (per-field breakdown).

The announcement finds that images lose metadata at about the same rate with or without a CDN, so that stripping appears to happen in the publishing pipeline and the fix is usually a setting, while the per-field page says publishers and CDNs discard it (IPTC announcement; per-field breakdown).
USA Today and Les Echos improved, the number of publishers keeping any metadata rose from 60 to 67 of 294, and France led the October country ranking (IPTC announcement).

Nearly half of publishers block an AI crawler in robots.txt, but the data-mining field is on 0.6% of images, 27 of 6,580 images carry a C2PA manifest, almost all signed by AI or design tools, and the AI fields the standard added in 2025 are nearly empty (IPTC announcement; per-field breakdown; Photo Metadata archive); the IPTC's 2026 conference focused on content provenance and the tracking of its real-world adoption (IPTC).

The announcement explains the problem as credits lost between camera and reader through re-encoding, resizing and optimisation, and says embedded metadata is often the only record of an image's origin and terms once it is copied or crawled for AI; its first results show little change since 2018 (IPTC announcement). USA Today and Les Echos improved, the number of publishers keeping any metadata rose from 60 to 67 of 294, and France led the October country ranking (IPTC announcement). Its stated limits are publishers blocking automated access, as AP and USA Today did in October, and publishers returning no photograph, listed as no_images (IPTC announcement; overview). L_BA.text: IPTC Metawatch is the International Press Telecommunications Council's free, open monitor of whether news publishers keep the credits, captions and rights information embedded in their photographs, checked every month across more than 500 publishers in 122 countries (IPTC announcement, 5 October 2026); the provenance census record types it as a monitor of the media lineage whose capability is to test, its provenance object 'the lead photograph of a news article, as served to the reader', its operator the IPTC at metawatch.iptc.org (provenance census record). Its own overview states the object from the side of the carrier: Metawatch 'tracks how often major news publishers preserve embedded photo metadata' — Exif, IPTC Photo Metadata in its IIM and XMP forms, and C2PA — and scores the photographs a curated list of publishers serves (Metawatch overview), the carrier the census record names as 'embedded metadata (Exif, IPTC IIM and XMP) and C2PA manifests' (provenance census record). Content Credentials stand in the first of the dimensions of provenance the archive's provenance packet distinguishes: frameworks for the artifact (C2PA / Content Credentials) and for the corpus 'are not designed to address the survival of authorial lineage through AI synthesis', artifact provenance verifying that 'this file' was created by 'this source' at 'this time', at the moment of creation (#725); the same packet places IPTC AI metadata at 'Layer 1 metadata', 'Disclosure, not lineage' (#725). On the first of each month its crawler visits 508 news publishers in 122 countries, takes up to 20 recent articles from each and reads the lead photograph of every article, checking Exif, IPTC Photo Metadata and C2PA Content Credentials and scoring creator, caption, copyright and credit line, 'the “4 Cs”' (IPTC announcement); the census record's unit is 'a news publisher, sampled each month through up to 20 recent articles', its count 508 publishers in 122 countries as of October 2026, monthly on the first, its relation types creator, credit, copyright, caption, the PLUS data-mining preference and Content Credentials (provenance census record); the per-field page calls the four scored fields 'the "Four Cs" of news photo provenance', the others tracked for context (Metawatch per-field breakdown). The crawler is 'deliberately light', about 40 to 60 requests per publisher a month, honouring robots.txt and keeping no article text or image files, and every run is published as open data under CC BY 4.0, new results appearing on the first of every month (IPTC announcement); the overview names it 'A project of the International Press Telecommunications Council', its data CC BY 4.0, with an opt-out for publishers by email (Metawatch overview), and the census record carries 'every run published as open data' under 'CC BY 4.0 (each run's data)' (provenance census record). What it tests is a transformation: credits 'are lost between camera and reader' as content management systems re-encode images, delivery networks resize them and optimisation tools discard what looks like unnecessary bytes, and once an image is copied or collected by an AI crawler its embedded metadata 'is often the only record of where it came from and on what terms it may be used' (IPTC announcement); the census record names the transformation tested 'publication through a news site's pipeline (CMS, CDN, image optimisation)' (provenance census record). The archive's packet states the loss one layer on: 'A C2PA-signed image whose caption is rewritten by a model that strips the photographer's name has lost semantic provenance even though artifact provenance is preserved', the dimensions being independent, so that 'Solving any one dimension does not solve the others' (#725). Metawatch builds on IMATAG's 2018 State of Image Metadata study and the IPTC's own prototype crawler of 2019, and differs in measuring every month (IPTC announcement; the census record quotes the sentence as its lineage evidence, provenance census record), and the census record relates it as part of the IPTC's photo-metadata tests, beside the census's C2PA conformance entry, while keeping it apart from the earlier test: 'NOT the 2019 IPTC social-media test: it measures news publishers monthly' (provenance census record). Its overview dates five runs, the first on 2026-06-03 and then monthly to 2026-10-01 (Metawatch overview), and the announcement counts 294 publishers 'measured every month since June' (IPTC announcement). The IPTC's post of 8 September 2026 reports that at the 2026 Photo Metadata Conference, held 'Last Thursday', Brendan Quinn 'appeared again to introduce Metawatch', 'IPTC’s new public service that monitors real-world usage of metadata in images across the global news industry, tracking IPTC/XMP, C2PA, AI opt-outs and more' (IPTC, 8 September 2026); Paul Melcher's LinkedIn post of 14 September 2026, read by its card alone, says the IPTC 'now publishes Metawatch' (LinkedIn card); the conference took as its focus AI transparency and content provenance, 'tracking real-world adoption of content transparency technologies by AI engines, news sites, software and services' (IPTC, 8 September 2026). The announcement is dated 5 October 2026 and is the newest post under the IPTC's Photo Metadata tag (IPTC announcement; Photo Metadata archive); the census record's lifecycle is active, 'announced 5 October 2026', its founding given the same way, the run reported for October 2026 and the record read on 2026-10-29 (provenance census record). The Capture Registry records the difference: the record 'dates the monitor by its announcement, 5 October 2026', two cards date it earlier, the IPTC post of 8 September and Melcher's post of 14 September, and the September showing is carried at the capture 'unchecked against the posts themselves' (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29). In the October run 7.2% of editorial images carried a credit or copyright notice, against IMATAG's 8% in 2018, so that keeping the photographer's credit attached 'has not improved'; 321 of the 425 publishers it could crawl kept none of the scored IPTC fields; 11% of 6,580 images carried any IPTC metadata, the photographer's name on 7.9%, the credit line on 5.7%, copyright on 5.6% (IPTC announcement); the census record's retention results carry the 7.2% and the 321 of 425 with the 27 of 6,580 images bearing a C2PA manifest (provenance census record), and the announcement reads its first results as showing 'how little has changed since 2018' and why metadata 'matters more than ever now that AI companies are crawling the web' (IPTC announcement). The overview gives the latest run as 2026-10-01, 425 sites, 122 countries and 6,580 images, a mean IPTC score of 5.96, 11% with any IPTC and 0.5% with C2PA, and says that 'Any average describes almost nobody here' (Metawatch overview); the per-field page counts over 6,514 images, Creator at 7.9%, CreditLine 5.7%, Copyright 5.3%, CaptionDescription 5%, the licensing fields below 3% (Metawatch per-field breakdown), so that copyright stands at 5.6% in the announcement and at 5.3% on the per-field page. On where the loss happens the operator's pages differ in emphasis: the announcement finds 'It isn’t the CDN’s fault', images through Cloudflare, Akamai, CloudFront and Fastly losing their metadata 87% to 95% of the time and images with no CDN 87%, so that 'Stripping appears to happen in the publishing pipeline', the fix 'usually a setting, not a project' (IPTC announcement; the census record quotes the pipeline sentence as its evidence, provenance census record), while the per-field page reads its dataset as 'publishers and CDNs are discarding metadata that the photographers and agencies almost certainly embedded upstream' (Metawatch per-field breakdown). The archive's specification for machine-eligible handwritten artifacts embeds IPTC Creator (the author or heteronym), Credit, CopyrightNotice, Headline, Description and DateCreated in every published derivative, with an XMP mirror and C2PA manifests wrapping the IPTC/EXIF assertions (#1409); it records embedded IPTC photo metadata as extracted by Google and travelling with the image, its composition role unknown, 'scaffold the pipeline provably reads' (#1409); and it carries the same fields in a visible membrane because 'physically embodied metadata survives screenshot, rehosting, filename change, metadata stripping, PDF embedding, and sidecar loss', under a triple redundancy of pixels, embedded IPTC/XMP/C2PA and external records (#1409). The archive's identifier stamp for a lossless image sits in its EXIF ImageDescription or UserComment (#1432), and its self-audit protocol plans a 'Hash/signature manifest (C2PA-compatible) binding provenance claims to deposited objects' (#204). Some publishers moved: USA Today from no credit metadata in 2019 to 95% of its lead photographs carrying credit, creator and copyright in September, Les Echos from 6% to 75%, and across the 294 publishers measured monthly since June those keeping any metadata rose from 60 to 67; France led October at 19.8 of 100, ahead of Germany at 19.2, with only countries of more than three scored publishers ranked (IPTC announcement). Of 505 publishers whose policies were checked, 234 block at least one AI crawler in robots.txt, but 'robots.txt protects a website, not a photograph', and the PLUS Data Mining field appears on 0.6% of images (IPTC announcement); the archive's training-layer protocol holds that robots.txt and C2PA, which it does not call useless, operate 'primarily at the publication / legal / evidentiary layer rather than at the training-survival layer' (#127). Leaving out the IPTC's own site, 27 of 6,580 images carried a C2PA manifest, all but one signed by an AI or design tool and none 'from a camera or a newsroom’s own signing', and seven carried a Digital Source Type disclosing generative-AI editing, so that, in the announcement's reading, provenance in news photography 'is arriving first through the tools that make synthetic images' (IPTC announcement); the per-field page finds DigitalSourceType on 0.2% of images and the AI prompt and AI system fields on none (Metawatch per-field breakdown), properties the IPTC Photo Metadata Standard added for AI-generated content on 27 November 2025 (Photo Metadata archive). The archive's packet calls the adoption of artifact authenticity 'uneven' and C2PA's ingredient assertions 'optional, under-adopted' (#725), and its field manual holds that C2PA standards and watermarking have not 'achieved sufficient adoption to function as infrastructure' (#499). The archive reads C2PA's trust as a device's: C2PA 'attests what a device reports having done' where a content-derived identifier 'computes what the bytes are', validation optional in the first, the two complementary (#1443), C2PA anchoring in device and issuer certificates and the AXN regime in content derivation and a public ledger (#1409), C2PA securing 'the camera's testimony, not the author's' (#1444). It declares a nonsynthetic capture by the IPTC DigitalSourceType inside the file, 'in the same controlled vocabulary whose trainedAlgorithmicMedia value marks the synthetic class', and holds that 'C2PA, FADGI, and IPTC provenance vocabularies are the same insight arriving as standards' (#1409). The monitor states its limits: the United States slipped from first to fourth in October because AP and USA Today 'began blocking automated access this month', 'a reminder that bot-blocking aimed at AI also shuts out research' (IPTC announcement; quoted in the census record's evidence, provenance census record), and publishers reached without a photograph are listed as no_images rather than scored zero, 'usually our blind spot rather than their practice' (Metawatch overview); the census record leaves unchecked 'the Metawatch site itself and its published run data' and IMATAG's 2018 study, and marks the monitor 'NOT a C2PA verifier' (provenance census record). The archive holds the artifact dimension necessary and insufficient: C2PA 'prevents forgery; it does not constitute authorship' (#729), 'C2PA authenticates media' and does not cover text (#621), and 'When a 5,000-word article becomes a 200-word AI Overview, C2PA cannot tell you what was lost' (#615). It finds that metadata standards, C2PA among them, do not address the measurable reception consequences of provenance and attribution (#833), that provenance and attribution studies, C2PA among them, 'have focused on attribution loss in AI outputs' (#1003), and that cross-format content provenance standards give 'starting points for the public and machine-readable layers' (#95). On Google's AI Overview, signed out, on 2026-10-29, the Capture Registry finds the method and scale right ('Every month', 'more than 500 news publishers in 122 countries' and the fields are the announcement's own) and 'Free and open' matched to the census record's licence quote, checked against that record and the pages it saved (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29). It finds the findings absent, 'The composition gives what the monitor checks and none of what it found', and the access limit not composed; it reads the Overview first as naming 'the maker, the method and the scale of a monitor three weeks old', then as composing 'A new provenance monitor' 'at the grain of its feature list', when what it measures is 'the erasure of credit in the publishing pipeline', carrying 'the instrument' and leaving out 'its reading', the IPTC photo metadata capture's pattern 'in small: the carrier composed, the loss omitted' (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29). At the capture the IPTC is named, Paul Melcher and Brendan Quinn appear only in cards, no identifier is given and the monitor's own pages are cited, and no card cites the census record, which landed on provenanceerasure.org the same day (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29). The census record asks of each entity 'What provenance does this system carry, through which operation, on whose assertion, with what evidence of survival?', each quote verbatim from a saved source, and for Metawatch read one source, the announcement, on 2026-10-29 (provenance census record); Wikipedia has no article on IPTC Metawatch and no article text naming it beside the IPTC, and its article on the operator, which does not name Metawatch, describes the IPTC as 'a consortium of the world's major news agencies, other news providers and news industry vendors' acting as 'the global standards body of the news media', whose photo metadata, the IIM set that XMP has largely superseded, is 'by far IPTC's most widely used standard' (Wikipedia).

translation.received: F1 (B1, announcement, standfirst ¶1): "The IPTC has launched Metawatch , a free, open monitor that checks every month whether more than 500 news publishers in 122 countries keep the credits, captions and rights information embedded in their photographs."; F21 (B2, overview, opening): "Metawatch tracks how often major news publishers preserve embedded photo metadata (Exif, IPTC Photo Metadata (in both original IIM format and newer XMP format), and C2PA) on the images they publish. We crawl a curated list of publishers monthly and score the photographs they serve."

translation.lineage: the method: the lead photograph of up to 20 articles from each of 508 publishers, scored on the 4 Cs
translation.received: F5 (B1, 'What Metawatch does' ¶1 s1–2): "Metawatch checks every month: does the photo metadata survive publication? On the first of each month our well-behaved crawler visits 508 news publishers in 122 countries, takes up to 20 recent articles from each, and reads the lead photograph of every article."; F6 (B1, 'What Metawatch does' ¶1 s3): "It checks each image for Exif, IPTC Photo Metadata (in both IIM and XMP form) and C2PA Content Credentials, and scores how each site carry the fields that matter most: creator, caption, copyright and credit line (the “4 Cs”)."; F28 (B4, per-field page, ¶2): "The "scored" badge marks the four fields that contribute to a site's overall score (the "Four Cs" of news photo provenance); the others are tracked for context but don't affect the score"

translation.lineage: open data, cadence and the operator

How it works is documented in full, and every run is published as open data under CC BY 4.0, so anyone can check our numbers or ask their own questions."; F19 (B1, closing ¶): "Metawatch automatically publishes new results on the first of every month."; F26 (B2, footer): "Metawatch · A project of the International Press Telecommunications Council . translation.lineage: the operator: the IPTC and its photo metadata standard
translation.received: F33 (B5, ¶1 s3): "This year we focussed on the industry’s implementation of recent legislation around AI transparency and content provenance, tracking real-world adoption of content transparency technologies by AI engines, news sites, software and services."; F35 (B6, tag archive, title and newest post): "Photo Metadata Archives - IPTC … Oct 5 2026 … Announcing Metawatch: a monthly check on which news publishers keep photo metadata"; F39 (B8, lead ¶1): "The International Press Telecommunications Council ( IPTC ), based in London , United Kingdom , is a consortium of the world's major news agencies , other news providers and news industry vendors and acts as the global standards body of the news media."; F40 (B8, 'Photo metadata' ¶1–2): "The IPTC defined a set of metadata properties that can be applied to images, part of a broader standard developed in the early 1990s and known as the IPTC Information Interchange Model (IIM). … The Extensible Metadata Platform (XMP) has largely superseded IIM's image file header structure"; F41 (B8, 'Photo metadata' ¶3): "Because of its nearly universal acceptance among photographers — even amateurs — this is by far IPTC's most widely used standard."
translation.translation: untranslated: composed as received beside PE-12, PE-20, PE-21, PE-22

translation.lineage: findings: credit and the scored fields (October 2026)
translation.received: F9 (B1, 'What we found' ¶1): "In 2018 IMATAG found that 8% of editorial images carried a credit or copyright notice. Applying the same test to our October run gives 7.2%. Whatever else has changed in news publishing since then, keeping the photographer’s credit attached to the photograph has not improved."; F10 (B1, 'What we found' ¶2): "In the October run, 321 of the 425 publishers we could crawl, three out of four kept none of the IPTC fields we score on any image we sampled. Only 11% of the 6,580 images carried any IPTC metadata at all . The field that survives most often is the photographer’s name, on just 7.9% of images; the credit line is on 5.7% and copyright on 5.6%."; F2 (B1, announcement, standfirst ¶2): "The first results show how little has changed since 2018, which publishers have fixed their sites, and why keeping metadata matters more than ever now that AI companies are crawling the web."; F22 (B2, overview, run summary): "Latest run 2026-10-01 Sites crawled 425 Countries 122 Images analysed 6,580 … Mean IPTC score 5.96 … % with any IPTC 11% % with C2PA 0.5%"; F24 (B2, overview, 'How the scores are distributed'): "Any average describes almost nobody here: a small group embed metadata thoroughly, and 321 of 425 publishers embed none we can find at all."; F29 (B4, per-field page, table rows (Field, Type, Present, Total, Population, Score weight)): "Creator scored 517 6,514 7.9% 25% … CreditLine scored 373 6,514 5.7% 25% … Copyright scored 348 6,514 5.3% 25% … CaptionDescription scored 324 6,514 5% 25%"
translation.translation: untranslated: composed as received beside PE-09

translation.lineage: where the stripping happens: the publishing pipeline
translation.received: F31 (B4, per-field page, 'What this tells us'): "Even the best-populated field — Creator at 7.9% — appears on fewer than one in ten images we fetched. The fields most relevant to licensing ( WebStatement , LicensorURL ) are below 3%. The dataset as a whole tells a consistent story: publishers and CDNs are discarding metadata that the photographers and agencies almost certainly embedded upstream."; F11 (B1, 'What we found' ¶3): "It isn’t the CDN’s fault. Images served through Cloudflare, Akamai, CloudFront and Fastly lost their metadata 87% to 95% of the time, but images served with no CDN at all also lost metadata 87% of the time. Stripping appears to happen in the publishing pipeline, which means that publishers can fix it."; F18 (B1, 'What publishers can do' ¶1 s1–2): "The fix is usually a setting, not a project. Most image pipelines strip metadata by default to save a few kilobytes; most can be told to keep it."
translation.translation: untranslated: composed as received beside PE-19

translation.lineage: AI: crawler blocking, the data-mining field, Content Credentials, the AI fields
translation.received: F15 (B1, 'AI: a locked front door, an open back door' ¶1–2): "Of the 505 publishers whose policies we checked, 234 (46%) block at least one AI crawler in their robots.txt. … But robots.txt protects a website, not a photograph. … IPTC Photo Metadata has a field for exactly this: PLUS Data Mining . Only 15 publishers (3.0%) put it on any image we sampled, and it appears on 0.6% of images overall."; F16 (B1, 'AI: a locked front door, an open back door' ¶3 s1–2): "Leaving out IPTC’s own site, 27 of the 6,580 images we analysed carried a C2PA manifest, and all but one were signed by an AI or design tool: OpenAI, Adobe, Canva or Google (the last had a signer we couldn’t read). None came from a camera or a newsroom’s own signing."; F17 (B1, 'AI: a locked front door, an open back door' ¶3 s3–4): "Seven images carried an IPTC Digital Source Type saying they had been edited with generative AI, which is exactly the kind of disclosure the field was designed for. Provenance in news photography is arriving first through the tools that make synthetic images, not through the photojournalism that most needs it."; F30 (B4, per-field page, table rows (AI fields)): "DigitalSourceType tracked 15 6,514 0.2% … AIPromptInformation tracked 0 6,514 0% … AISystemUsed tracked 0 6,514 0%"; F36 (B6, tag archive, post of 27 November 2025): "Nov 27 2025 … IPTC Photo Metadata Standard adds new properties for AI-generated content"
translation.translation: untranslated: composed as received beside O127-01

translation.lineage: stated limits: access blocked, the crawler's blind spots
translation.received: F14 (B1, 'Which countries do best' ¶2 (after the chart)): "The United States led in September and slipped to fourth in October, but only because two of its best-scoring publishers were out of reach: AP and USA Today began blocking automated access this month. It is a reminder that bot-blocking aimed at AI also shuts out research."; F25 (B2, overview, 'How the scores are distributed', note): "Publishers we reached but got no photograph from are listed separately as no_images rather than scored zero, since that is usually our blind spot rather than their practice."
